title: Gradients with a numerical check
goals: Estimate one partial derivative while other parameters stay fixed
Assemble a gradient in a declared parameter order
Compare numerical and formula based gradients with a tolerance

prerequisite.prompt: Why is the symmetric-slope denominator twice the step?
prerequisite.answer: The two evaluation points lie one step on either side of the centre, so their separation is two steps.

vocabulary: A local slope with respect to one parameter while others are held fixed
The ordered vector of partial derivatives of a scalar function
An estimate of change computed from nearby function values
A stated allowance for numerical disagreement

lesson.title: Vary one parameter at a time

blocks.text: Use one example with input x = 2 and target t = 3. The model predicts y = wx + b, and loss L(w, b) = (2w + b - 3) squared. At w = 1, b = 0, prediction is 2, residual is -1 and loss is 1. There are two parameters in order [w, b].

To estimate the partial slope for w, change w only and keep b = 0. To estimate the partial slope for b, change b only and keep w = 1. Moving both at once measures change along a combined direction; it does not isolate either partial derivative.
The gradient is [-4, -2] in order [w, b]. Both entries refer to the same original parameter vector, not to a partially updated model.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def loss(w, b):
    return (2 * w + b - 3) ** 2

def gradient_check(w, b, step=0.001):
    dw = (loss(w + step, b) - loss(w - step, b)) / (2 * step)
    db = (loss(w, b + step) - loss(w, b - step)) / (2 * step)
    residual = 2 * w + b - 3
    formula = [4 * residual, 2 * residual]
    numerical = [dw, db]
    assert all(abs(a - n) < 1e-6
               for a, n in zip(formula, numerical))
    return numerical

print([round(g, 6) for g in gradient_check(1, 0)])
# [-4.0, -2.0]

The helper assumes finite numerical inputs and a positive nonzero step. The formula follows the squared-loss rule: local loss change is twice the residual times the prediction sensitivity. Changing w by a small amount changes prediction twice as much here; changing b changes prediction by the same amount.

Exact floating-point equality is not required. Record the step and a tolerance, then try more than one parameter setting. A passing numerical check supports agreement for those tested points; it does not prove all possible inputs.

blocks.title: Two separate probes at one parameter vector
blocks.caption: The first two rows are independent local probes, not successive parameter updates. The final row records both results in the declared order.

blocks.label: At w = 0, b = 1, find prediction, residual, loss and the gradient using [4 times residual, 2 times residual].

lesson.title: Choose checks away from sharp corners

blocks.text: ReLU is not differentiable exactly at zero. A symmetric difference across that corner can average two different behaviours. When checking a network gradient, use points whose relevant scores are safely away from zero, and check that the small perturbations do not cross a corner. Document any derivative convention used at zero.

At the centre of the simple scalar ReLU function, [ReLU(0.1) - ReLU(-0.1)] / 0.2 equals 0.5. This symmetric number does not make the function differentiable at zero. Also avoid assuming an ever-smaller step is always better: subtraction and rounding can spoil numerical differences.

lesson.title: Use the gradient as local evidence

blocks.text: The gradient describes how the stated loss changes near the current parameters. For a differentiable function, moving a sufficiently small distance opposite a nonzero gradient decreases the function locally. The gradient alone does not choose a safe finite step, establish a global minimum or demonstrate generalisation.

blocks.label: A numerical checker moves w and b together, gets one slope and copies it into both gradient entries. What is wrong with this check?

blocks.text: Next week combines a gradient with an explicit learning rate to update parameters together.

workbook.title: Recover a gradient
workbook.prompt: For the lesson model at w = 1 and b = 1, calculate prediction, residual, loss and gradient.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Prediction 3, residual 0, loss 0, gradient [0, 0].

workbook.title: Catch a denominator error
workbook.prompt: A w probe has losses 1.44 and 0.64 at 0.9 and 1.1 with b fixed. A learner divides their difference by 0.1. Correct the result.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The interval is 0.2. (0.64 - 1.44) / 0.2 = -4, not -8.

workbook.title: Separate a direction from a coordinate
workbook.prompt: Starting at [w, b] = [1, 0], both coordinates move by plus or minus 0.1 together. Compute the symmetric slope and explain why it is not either partial derivative.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals are -1.3 and -0.7; losses 1.69 and 0.49. Slope is -6. It measures the combined direction [1, 1], equal here to the sum of partials -4 and -2.

workbook.title: Check a new example independently
workbook.prompt: Use x = 3, target 2 and y = wx + b at w = 0, b = 1. With step 0.1, calculate both numerical partials. Compare with [2 times residual times x, 2 times residual].
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residual -1 and loss 1. w probes give predictions 0.7 and 1.3, losses 1.69 and 0.49, partial -6. b probes give predictions 0.9 and 1.1, losses 1.21 and 0.81, partial -2. Formula gradient is [-6, -2].

workbook.title: Recognise a corner
workbook.prompt: Compute the symmetric difference of ReLU at zero with step 0.1. Explain why this does not prove a derivative exists there.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The value is 0.5. The left slope is 0 and right slope is 1, so the slopes disagree and the derivative at zero does not exist.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to separate coordinate probes from combined changes. The first gradient check is deliberately an affine model with squared loss, avoiding hidden-layer calculus. Introduce the chain-rule reasoning in words before showing the compact formula.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the symmetric denominator and compute the initial prediction and residual.
Probe w alone with b fixed; record the two losses and slope.
Probe b alone and assemble [-4, -2]. Complete W1 and W2.
Trace the optional numerical checker and the guided [0, 1] case.
Use W3 to distinguish a combined direction from two partial derivatives.
Discuss the ReLU corner in W5 and a stated numerical tolerance.
Collect W4 independently, requiring both pairs of losses and coordinate order.
Use the exit response and fresh retry, then connect local gradient evidence to next week.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: prediction 1, residual -2, loss 4, gradient [-8, -4]. Exit: changing both parameters measures a directional change; each partial must vary just its own coordinate while holding the others fixed.
misconceptions: It has one entry per parameter for a scalar loss, in a stated order.
Use the updated weight for the bias probe
Both entries must refer to the same current parameter vector.
A symmetric value defines the derivative at any corner
Left and right slopes can differ; the ReLU example exposes this.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires numerical and formula gradients [-6, -2] with losses shown. Fresh retry: x = 1, target 4, w = 2, b = 1 gives residual -1 and gradient [-2, -2]. Step 0.1 in either coordinate gives losses 1.21 and 0.81. Require the fixed coordinate to be named.
teacher.support: Provide separate w-probe and b-probe tables. Extension: at the lesson model [1, 0], test steps 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 and report absolute disagreements from [-4, -2], without claiming universal tolerance guarantees.
